title: Inside Clio's AI-Driven Transformation: CPO John Foreman and CTO Jonathan Watson
author: John Foreman · Jonathan Watson

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: The source shifts attention from lawyer-led learning, governance and public-interest participation to Clio’s provider-side priorities: rapid product execution, security, compliance and anticipated product maturity. It does not oppose professional engagement, but it advances a materially different, vendor-execution framing and offers no evidence that lawyers are shaping deployment.

st.an: The source focuses on product integration and proactive AI workflows, not on associate apprenticeship, verification competence, mentorship, simulation or the reproduction of legal expertise. It therefore provides insufficient evidence to determine a position on the cluster’s proposition.

st.t: Legal workflows: Contextual agents remain lawyer-guided
st.an: The introduction gestures toward Clio’s integration of legal-research assets into an AI-enabled legal work platform, which is relevant to the cluster’s connected-platform theme. st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s hybrid, workflow-oriented view by treating AI as a legal-work teammate rather than autonomous legal delivery. It materially extends the institutional-absorption point by arguing that proactive workflows require integrated access to the firm’s software and information, illustrated by pre-consult intake and timeline preparation. These are proposed capabilities, not measured evidence, and the source does not address verification or accountability.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s workflow-redesign proposition and materially extends it with a concrete platform strategy: connect AI across end-to-end legal workflows while preserving role-based interfaces, enterprise permissions, integration and iterative customer-led deployment. It is less informative on verification and measured capability limits.

kp.k: AI enables integration across previously separate legal software categories
kp.d: CTO Jonathan Watson describes AI as the technological basis for combining business operations, substantive legal practice and research into workflows rather than launching separate lines of business. He argues that document drafting requires legal research and intake requires practice-management information. This is Clio's product-strategy account, not a measured finding about outcomes.
qs: So instead of thinking of them as discrete things, we begin to think about it as a set of capabilities that we bring to bear to do actual work

that's the large transformational change that's happening inside of Clio is just thinking less in these slices and just workflows and work and automations and action across everything that an attorney or user needs.

kp.k: Vertical software supplies context and tools for AI action
kp.d: CPO John Foreman argues that industry-specific software gives AI access to customer context across front- and back-office operations, enabling it to execute tasks rather than merely provide information. His proposed advantage concerns software vendors' ability to connect data and actions throughout the client journey.
qs: the best AI is AI where like, it understands the whole context and it can do things. And that really comes from vertical software.
I understand the information because I operate the back office. I operate the front office, right?
I can actually like do a thing, like run intake or assemble a bill or collect payment.

kp.k: AI teammates could prepare work across the client journey
kp.d: Foreman uses the analogy of a human teammate moving between tools to explain cross-product AI coordination. His illustrative personal-injury workflow has AI process intake documents into a timeline before the consultation. The claim is prospective: shared access could let AI anticipate subsequent work, rather than confining it to a single application.
qs: Real teammates, they're constantly like, maybe they got two monitors, maybe they got a swivel chair, but they're constantly those. They're moving stuff around.
maybe I should put this into a timeline. I can go ahead and do that. And that way that timeline's maybe ready even at the consult call, right?
a good teammate would probably get ahead on some things.

kp.k: Bounded automation retains attorney approval in an illustrative workflow
kp.d: Watson recounts an unresolved request to change his own retainer agreement after about eight days and proposes AI redrafting the relevant provision, presenting it to the attorney for approval, and handling subsequent execution steps. Foreman separately rejects uncontrolled autonomy in favor of specific, incremental interventions. These are augmentation examples and design intentions, not evidence of deployed autonomous legal representation.
qs: That entire loop I still have not resolved and it's been like eight days.
I would love for AI to pick up that communication, redraft that part of it and pop to the attorney and say, is this all right?

And it doesn't mean like, go crazy, send some autonomous thing off to get you sued for malpractice. It means identifying very specific moments that's like, I can move the ball forward a couple of yards here for you.

kp.k: Systems of action build on systems of record
kp.d: Foreman characterizes the transition as moving from storing matters, contacts, documents and expenses to performing intake, scheduling, time tracking and research. Watson identifies the technology developed for Duo, unified product data and access across systems as foundations. Their argument is that execution depends on existing records rather than replacing their importance.
qs: Not waiting for you to do it and then you put the thing you did in it. What can it do?
We're switching from like nouns to verbs.
Now, can't do any of the verbs without the nouns, right?
pulling together all the data into a single place, giving access to it for all these various systems.

kp.k: Clio Work extends the offering into substantive legal production
kp.d: The host introduces Clio Work as an AI workspace for research, reasoning and drafting. Foreman places it alongside firm growth and operational management as a third product pillar focused on substantive work product, bringing together drafting, a legal library and Vincent legal-research AI. The positioning expands Clio's software offering into producing legal work; it is not a claim that Clio itself delivers legal services.
qs: One of Clio's major new product announcements at Clio Con was Clio Work, an AI workspace for research, reasoning, and drafting.
Let's gather Draft together with a library, with a legal research AI like Vincent, and let's really help people assemble that product

kp.k: AI integration coexists with separately purchased product capabilities
kp.d: The host describes Clio Work as a separate product costing $199 a month. Foreman explains that a Manage customer can buy Manage AI for functions such as scheduling-order processing and automatic bill assembly, while substantive research and other Work capabilities require buying Work. He anticipates cross-product prompts encouraging those purchases; integration therefore does not mean every capability is included in one subscription.

I can buy Manage AI, right?
That includes things like, we talked about yesterday, processing scheduling orders, right?

kp.k: Task-specific workspaces constrain and coordinate AI
kp.d: Foreman describes humans and AI using the same product tools, with agents coordinating jobs across product boundaries—for example, moving from intake to research on custody and domestic violence. Watson argues that knowing the user's task allows tailored solutions and narrows the problem space compared with a general-purpose AI expected to do everything. These are design rationales rather than benchmarked quality claims.

when you walk into work we know what you're there to do and That allows us to build a bunch of tailored solutions to doing that very specific job

kp.k: Product boundaries balance integration against interface complexity
kp.d: Foreman reports conflicting customer preferences: some want a unified product, while others want a simpler point solution. He says Clio separates products around employees' roles and working modes to avoid excessive interface complexity, while AI can move across those divisions. This is a vendor account of design trade-offs and customer feedback, without survey evidence.
qs: we do have customers that are like, this should just all be one product.
this interface is too complex, you got too much shit in here, I don't use, I just want this.
They might actually be a different employee than the things that are in managed. So that felt like a good dividing line.
Now when it comes to AI, AI can actually move across those things.

kp.k: Enterprise expansion requires customization and distinct buyer-user considerations
kp.d: Discussing Clio Operate and the move upmarket, Watson emphasizes scale, process enforcement and integration of point solutions rather than a fundamentally different technology problem. Foreman identifies customization, separation between purchasers and daily users, and substantial internal operational requirements as enterprise challenges. He argues that adapting an existing small-firm product upmarket is advantageous; this is an executive judgment, not comparative market evidence.
qs: I need to operate more at scale. I need more customized ability to enforce my practices, processes.
You might need to weave together a wide variety of point solutions inside of an enterprise verb in a way that you probably don't in a solo or something else.
In enterprise, the people who buy the software and purchase the software and the people who use the software are actually different folks.
we'll have to build a certain level of customizability into the software.

kp.k: Acquisition integration and product maturity remain ongoing commitments
kp.d: The host places the interview at ClioCon in Boston in October 2025 and reports that the billion-dollar vLex acquisition was not closed during the conversation but closed a few weeks later. Foreman frames the announcements as a starting line and predicts that many discussed capabilities will be fully developed by the following year's conference; Watson emphasizes speed alongside security and compliance. These forward-looking commitments should not be read as completed capabilities at interview time.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Foreman and Watson argue that context-rich, integrated AI can perform work across intake, practice management, research and drafting, rather than merely store information.
pts.d: Foreman claims that vertical legal software gives AI the information and operational access needed to conduct intake, assemble bills and collect payments. Watson describes AI as enabling Clio to connect previously separate business-of-law, practice-of-law and research capabilities. They present a shift from a system of record to a system that performs bounded actions. Foreman's prospective examples include preparing a personal-injury timeline before a consultation and orchestrating agents across products. Watson illustrates the proposed client-service benefits with an AI-assisted retainer revision that an attorney approves before completion. These are workflow claims and illustrative possibilities, not claims that lawyers will become unnecessary.

pts.k: Foreman positions Clio Work as an integrated substantive-work offering; Watson claims that task-specific context enables more tailored AI assistance.
pts.d: Foreman describes bringing drafting, a legal library and Vincent legal-research AI together to help lawyers assemble their substantive work product. He distinguishes AI capabilities within Grow, Manage and Work while proposing connections across those product boundaries. Watson argues that knowing the user's intended job within Work improves the specificity and quality of the solutions Clio can build. Access remains modular: Manage AI provides management-related assistance, while additional research or drafting workflows may require purchasing Work.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists of executive product-development experience, descriptions of technical foundations, and illustrative workflow anecdotes rather than measured outcomes.
pts.d: Foreman draws on his experience at horizontal software companies to explain his preference for context-rich vertical AI. Watson identifies Duo and the unification of Clio product data as foundations for the proposed capabilities. His unresolved retainer amendment supplies a personal example of friction that AI might reduce, not a completed AI implementation or demonstrated saving. The interview supplies no quantified productivity results, legal-quality benchmarks, accuracy measurements or controlled client-outcome evidence for the executives' claims. For enterprise development, Watson describes customer feedback, discovery and iterative deployment as the intended learning process.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The executives describe an ongoing rollout in October 2025, with Foreman expecting many discussed capabilities to be more fully developed by the following year's conference.
pts.d: Foreman treats the conference announcements as a starting line rather than a finished transformation and predicts that many discussed features will be fully developed by the next year's gathering, implying 2026. The proposed benefits depend on access to relevant matter data and tools, integration across products, and appropriate subscriptions. He explicitly limits the approach to specific workflow advances rather than unrestricted autonomy; Watson's retainer example includes attorney approval. Watson also identifies security and compliance as development requirements. At the interview, acquisition-related integration remained subject to regulatory constraints; the document's introductory note reports that the acquisition subsequently closed.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The proposed changes affect lawyers, law-firm staff and clients, with different deployment needs for solos and enterprise firms.
pts.d: Lawyers and staff are expected to receive assistance with intake, scheduling, billing, research and document production, reducing manual coordination and helping them complete specific jobs faster. Clients could experience shorter waits and less frustration, as illustrated by Watson's retainer example. Foreman notes that intake and management may involve different employees even where AI can cross the software boundaries. For larger firms, the executives identify requirements for scale, process customization, integration of point solutions, permissions and reporting. Foreman distinguishes solos, where software buyer and user coincide, from enterprise firms, where purchasing and daily use involve different people. The interview does not establish workforce reductions or access-to-justice outcomes.
